item.title: Is Romantic Openness Overrated?
item.description:
Relationships

Is Romantic Openness Overrated?

Complete transparency may undermine intimacy.

Posted October 31, 2026

Key points
  • We can be deeply known without being completely exposed.
  • True intimacy involves knowing what to share, when to share it, and what to keep private.
  • Openness strengthens love, but unfiltered transparency can undermine it.
  • Deep love means being known well while remaining fully oneself.

"A life spent entirely in public, in the presence of others, becomes shallow." — Hannah Arendt

Most people want a romantic partner who understands them deeply. Yet being fully understood can sometimes feel confining rather than liberating. Does a flourishing relationship require complete openness, or is there an optimal balance between openness and privacy?

The Fusion Model of Romantic Love

"I've got you so deep in my heart, that you're really a part of me." — Frank Sinatra

Popular romantic ideals often emphasize unity, even fusion, between lovers. Partners are portrayed as soulmates, two halves of the same whole who are "meant for each other." Romantic closeness is therefore associated with openness: The deeper the love, the more we are expected to reveal about ourselves.

This longing for fusion may be understood as a response to the fear of separation, making the beloved seem like an inseparable part of oneself. Yet such thinking can lead to a Siamese-twin model of intimacy, in which every significant movement of one partner involves the other. Profound romantic closeness is better understood as functional harmony than mechanical fusion. Lovers can be deeply connected without surrendering their individuality.

The Virtue of Privacy

"I don't agree that you have to tell your partner EXACTLY what you're engaged in online. My husband and I have agreed on boundary issues, and we agree that some things are private. He doesn't listen in on my phone calls, read my letters, or ask me what I'm doing in the bathroom for so long. I don't ask him if he got a lap dance from the stripper. I don't particularly want to know that he may masturbate to thoughts of my sister. Part of loving someone is accepting that they have 'a life' outside of what you share together, even in the area of sexuality." — A married woman

A couple fighting
Source: pexels-rada-aslanova-150604297-27222425

Privacy is commonly understood as the right to be left alone: the ability to pursue one's activities without unnecessary scrutiny or interference. In close relationships, privacy involves maintaining boundaries, whereas openness involves relaxing some of them.

Intimacy requires self-disclosure. We cannot become close to someone without sharing personal information and relinquishing some privacy. Yet intimacy does not require the elimination of privacy. Indeed, people sometimes disclose highly personal information to complete strangers precisely because those strangers play little role in their lives.

article continues after advertisement

The significance of disclosure depends not only on what we reveal but also on to whom we reveal it and the role that person occupies in our lives. There is therefore an inherent tension between intimacy and privacy. Greater intimacy often requires greater openness, but unlimited openness may threaten both autonomy and intimacy. The challenge is finding the right balance.

How Much Love Should Exist Between Romantic Partners?

"A woman may not tell her spouse about her extramarital affairs and sexual fantasies, while she may openly discuss such matters with her online friend." — Unknown

"Honesty has ruined more marriages than infidelity." — Charles McCabe

Romantic intimacy is closely associated with openness, honesty, and self-disclosure. Yet openness is not limitless. Romantic partners are not fused into one person. They remain distinct individuals whose private dreams, fantasies, memories, desires, and thoughts help shape their identities.

If everything is disclosed, nothing remains private. Openness can promote trust and authenticity, but unfiltered transparency may also be harmful. Telling a partner everything that crosses one's mind can be insensitive and hurtful. It may diminish some of the mystery and playfulness that nourish romantic attraction. Complete transparency can erode tact and discretion and sometimes foster disregard or even contempt.

article continues after advertisement

True intimacy is not simply a matter of reporting everything that occurs in one's mind. It also involves knowing what should be said, when it should be said, and what is better left unsaid. This insight is especially relevant during the early stages of a relationship and during periods of conflict. A passing fantasy, a momentary resentment, or an embarrassing desire does not necessarily warrant disclosure. Openness is an important tool for strengthening a romantic bond, but like any tool, it can become counterproductive when used indiscriminately. The question, then, is not whether partners should be open, but how much openness best serves the relationship.

Secrecy in Romantic Relationships

In their study of secrecy in intimate relationships, Christian Klesse and Jenn van Hooff (2025) argue that secrecy is an integral aspect of intimate life in both consensual non-monogamy (such as polyamory) and non-consensual non-monogamy (such as affairs). They note that some women describe secret affairs as the only practical way to preserve primary relationships that might otherwise collapse. Klesse and van Hooff suggest that secrecy is not always a sign of deception or ill will. In some circumstances, it can reflect concern for others through respect for privacy, personal boundaries, and relational stability.

This does not mean that secrecy is harmless or that deception should be encouraged. Rather, it suggests that privacy and secrecy should not be treated as moral equivalents. Privacy protects legitimate personal boundaries; secrecy may conceal information that a partner has a reasonable claim to know. The distinction is crucial.

Concluding Thoughts

"My wife of 26 years knows everything except some of my deepest, most perverted thoughts. If she knew those, she'd probably lose respect for me." — A man

"Obviously I am not going to offer information that would hurt him (i.e., I had a sex dream about an ex last night)." — A woman

The human mind is complex, containing beliefs, fantasies, and desires shaped by evolution, childhood, and later experience. People possess a remarkable capacity to imagine alternative romantic possibilities without wishing to act on them. A mature relationship distinguishes between what we think, what we desire, and what we choose to do. We should primarily be judged by our meaningful choices and actual behavior rather than by every fleeting fantasy that enters our minds. Revealing the entire contents of one's inner life does not necessarily provide a more accurate picture of one's character. Sometimes, it provides a distorted one (Ben-Ze'ev, 2019).

Romantic intimacy does not require the disappearance of privacy. However, too much privacy can undermine intimacy just as too much openness can. Wisdom lies in balance rather than in defending privacy per se. We can be deeply known without being completely exposed. Perhaps the deepest form of romantic closeness is not, "You know everything about me," but rather, "You know me deeply, and you still allow me to remain myself."

item.title: The Case for Kindness, Even When It is a Hard Call
item.description:
Happiness

The Case for Kindness, Even When It is a Hard Call

How kindness affects your physical and psychological health.

Posted October 31, 2026

Key points
  • Acts of kindness can range from small and simple to life-changing and complex.
  • Being nice in the workplace can help build your personal power.
  • Benefits of being kind include increased happiness, well-being, relationships, and better health.
Source: CreativeCanvasDesign/Pixabay

Most of us know what kindness is when we show it or when we see it. However the variety and scope of kind acts may be both smaller or greater than we typically consider. A smile or kind word may make someone’s day, a connection ever so brief, but a kind act that is meaningful in that moment. On the greater scale, kindness can be seen in efforts such as that by Bono, the lead singer of U2, who lobbied relentlessly and successfully for nations to provide AIDS/HIV medications that saved millions of African lives.

Writing for the Mayo Clinic, psychologist Steve Siegle described kindness as “a spirit of helpfulness, being generous and considerate, and doing so without expecting anything in return.” In Decoding the Workplace I shared that doing favors for others, such as in the workplace, builds personal power. This need not be manipulative or even intentional. Just being nice and helping others when they need help suffices. Just be kind.

Is Kindness a Trait, Attitude, or Behavior?

As a psychological concept, what is kindness? It may be viewed in different ways. For some it is a trait acquired over the years through our experiences and observations: “I like to think I am a kind person.” It can also be thought of as an attitude: “I like to do favors for others.” Accordingly the degree to which we are kind may vary across our lives. Ultimately our kindness is expressed through our behaviors, small and large, to help others. For example, earlier in my life I volunteered weekly at a children’s medical center doing research to help the parents of children and occasionally research for physicians.

Just because acts of kindness are done usually with no expected benefits in mind does not mean that acts of kindness are without benefits. To the contrary, research has shown numerous benefits. Multiple studies have found that being kind increases one’s happiness. Lee Rowland and Oliver Curry, published in The Journal of Social Psychology, stated “the more kindness activities that one does, the greater the increase in happiness.” It doesn’t matter whether the act is for a close friend or family member (strong ties) or a stranger (weak ties). Similarly studies have shown that acts of kindness increase well-being, both in Western cultures where people are more independent and in Eastern cultures where people are more interdependent.

How Does Kindness Affect Physical and Mental Health?

Kindness also benefits our body and mind through physiological effects. Increases in empathy, self-esteem, and mood can lower blood pressure and cortisol levels, thus reducing stress. Likewise acts of kindness can boost neurotransmitters like serotonin and dopamine enhancing positive feelings. In short, kindness activities can better our health. All other things being equal, the kind person should be healthier than the less kind person.

article continues after advertisement

Social connections are important to our mental health across our lifespans. Being kind to others creates opportunities to connect and build relationships. This, in turn, can help with issues of loneliness and disconnection.

Is it tough to be kind? At times it can be. Political discourse, family feuds, disagreements, there may be obstacles. But being tough enough to be kind can make a difference in our lives, others’ lives, our world. Steve Siegle ended his Mayo Clinic article with a quotation from the Dalai Lama. I close with that quotation: “Be kind whenever possible. It is always possible.”
